title: The animals with no spine
question: Why is having no backbone a handy label but a poor family tree?
hook: Most animals lack a backbone, but the group they form is not a real branch of life.
idea: Invertebrate names animals by what they lack, so it is a term of convenience that covers very different body plans.

beats.prompt: A tunicate has no backbone. Which animals are its closest relatives?

choices.label: Vertebrates, more closely than other invertebrates
Other invertebrates such as insects and snails
choices.feedback: It tempts because all of them lack a backbone, but tunicates are more closely related to vertebrates.

choices.label: Sponges, since both lack a vertebral column
choices.feedback: Lacking a backbone is only a shared absence, and it does not show close kinship.

beats.explain: Tunicates and cephalochordates are sister chordate subphyla to the vertebrates, which makes the grouping of invertebrates paraphyletic.

beats.prompt: Sort each animal by the kind of skeleton it has.
beats.explain: Many invertebrates, such as jellyfish and worms, have fluid-filled hydrostatic skeletons. Others, like insects and crustaceans, have hard outer exoskeletons.

beats.prompt: Match each invertebrate to its lopsided feature.
pairs: Breathing hole on the right side
One claw much larger than the other
Fixed in place with no symmetry
beats.explain: These animals show asymmetry, which is rare among animal body plans.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: Invertebrates are animals without a backbone.
Tunicates have no backbone, so they fit that description.
So tunicates must be more closely related to insects than to vertebrates.
So invertebrate marks one tidy branch of animal life.
beats.explain: Tunicates are actually more closely related to vertebrates than to other invertebrates. That is why the group is paraphyletic and not a true branch.
